equipmentIdentity.note: The institutional Deutsche Biographie entry for Kirchbach identifies the Prussian V Corps in the Third Army and its fighting at Wissembourg on 4 August 1870, explicitly alongside Bavarian troops. The infantry assault on the town, station and Geisberg establishes a Prussian infantry component. The GER 3RD ARMY aggregate remains mixed; Bavarian and other allied contingents are not renamed or assigned a Prussian national identity. The historical polity establishes equipment eligibility only; the local participant ID, collective name and every quantity are retained. The Souvenir Français inventory, p.130, independently reproduces the inscription for a major of the Royal Prussian 47th Infantry Regiment killed on 4 August 1870.

note:
Reviewed CDB90 match 220, pinned revision e0b35ec4d798cec3bb4e6970c0f6bb7aa69e2f4c. CDB90 (CAA Database of Battles, Version 1990), tidy data maintained by Jeffrey B. Arnold. Original US Army Concepts Analysis Agency data; revised data licensed ODC-BY. Original force designations and strength interpretations are retained with each quantity. Each side is one aggregate force, including any coalition; its total is not allocated among members. Personnel casualties are not deaths. Source estimates and adjudged error margins are not statistical confidence intervals. Equipment and tactical movements are not established by this dataset. Match review: Both formations remain local. GER 3RD ARMY is not silently assigned to the post-1871 German Empire.

The Musée de l’Armée campaign testimony names survivors of the 74th regiment from Douay’s division after Wissembourg, alongside tirailleurs. Le Souvenir Français records the surviving inscription identifying a sergeant-major of the 74th line regiment killed at Wissembourg. This establishes a line-infantry component, not the dress of the tirailleurs or the entire I Corps. The kepi, blue-grey campaign capote, garance trousers and Chassepot M1866 with sabre bayonet are a documented 1870 line-infantry analogy. Clothing, regiment, supply and branch varied; this is not a claim that every soldier of the mixed army wore or carried these items. Zouaves, tirailleurs, guards, mobiles, cavalry and artillery are not converted into line infantry. No component proportion, new participant, strength, loss or death is inferred. The Draner print used for visual corroboration was published in 1871; it is not dated to the battle and does not broaden the profile’s eligibility.

The institutional Deutsche Biographie entry for Kirchbach identifies the Prussian V Corps in the Third Army and its fighting at Wissembourg on 4 August 1870, explicitly alongside Bavarian troops. The infantry assault on the town, station and Geisberg establishes a Prussian infantry component. The GER 3RD ARMY aggregate remains mixed; Bavarian and other allied contingents are not renamed or assigned a Prussian national identity. The leather spiked helmet, blue tunic, grey trousers and Dreyse M1862 form a representative 1870 Prussian line-infantry analogy. Helmet patterns, regimental details, clothing and equipment varied. The Auxonne helmet is a surviving November 1870 trophy, not an object proven to have been at this battle; the Carnavalet print shows several forms of dress. No fixed bayonet or precise regimental badge is reconstructed. The equipment identity Q27306 is a gate for this reviewed component only. Existing participant IDs, names, aggregate membership, all strengths, losses and deaths remain unchanged; no infantry share is inferred. Cavalry, artillery, guards, riflemen and allied states are not recategorized as this line-infantry component. The Souvenir Français inventory, p.130, independently reproduces the inscription for a major of the Royal Prussian 47th Infantry Regiment killed on 4 August 1870.
